name: Investment Banking
summary: Investment banks advise companies, governments and investors on mergers and acquisitions and help them raise money by issuing debt and equity. They earn fees for finding investors and structuring deals.

guide.heading: How a bank is organised
items: Main divisions: Investment Banking (IBD), Sales & Trading, and Research. IBD is separated from the rest of the firm by an information barrier ("the wall").

Industry (coverage) groups focus on a sector: Consumer/Retail, Tech/Media/Telecom (TMT), Industrials, Natural Resources, Financial Institutions (FIG), Healthcare, Real Estate, Gaming & Lodging (REGL), and more.
Product groups focus on a type of deal: M&A, Equity Capital Markets (IPOs, follow-on offerings), Debt Capital Markets (refinancing, acquisition debt), and Leveraged Finance (high-yield debt).
A deal moves from pitching (pitch books, modeling and valuation) to execution, where coverage and product groups work together, and then to follow-up work.
Typical ladder: Analyst (2–3 years), Associate, Vice President (where the job shifts toward clients), Director, Managing Director.

guide.heading: Types of banks
items: Bulge bracket: Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JPMorganChase, Bank of America, Citi, Barclays, UBS, Wells Fargo.
Elite boutiques: Evercore, Lazard, Moelis, Centerview, PJT Partners, Perella Weinberg, Qatalyst.
Middle market: Jefferies, Houlihan Lokey, Harris Williams, William Blair, Baird, Lincoln International, Raymond James.

guide.heading: The analyst role
items: Building financial models in Excel, putting together pitch books, presenting analysis to senior bankers, and working with clients and executives.
Long hours, especially on live deals; days often run well into the night, with weekend work.

Why people choose IB: a strong foundation in modeling and valuation, deals with tangible results, early exposure to senior executives, and exits to private equity, venture capital, hedge funds, corporate finance, or promotion to Associate.

guide.heading: Early programs
items: Many banks run freshman and sophomore insight days, early-ID programs and fellowships. They often lead to interviews or fast-tracked internship applications.
Applications for sophomore programs usually close in the fall, and the programs themselves run over winter and early spring.
Since 2025 many banks have renamed their diversity programs or opened them to all applicants. Always check the current eligibility on the firm's page.
Track deadlines on the Programs tab, and pin the ones you want reminders for.

guide.heading: Networking
items: Reach out to Vanderbilt alumni and upperclassmen who have done IB internships. LinkedIn, BBSA events, the Career Center and Handshake events are good places to find them.
Go to firm info sessions and coffee chats. Research the person and their group before you meet, and come with questions.
Follow up with a short thank-you email within a day. The Email formats tab shows how each bank formats addresses.

guide.heading: Interviews
items: A common sequence: a HireVue or phone screen, a first round, then a Superday of 3–5 back-to-back interviews.
Behavioral: "Walk me through your resume", "Why investment banking?", "Why our bank?", plus teamwork and leadership stories.

Technical: the main valuation methods and which gives the highest value, walking through a DCF (WACC, CAPM, beta), how the three financial statements connect, EBITDA, LBO basics, and enterprise value vs. equity value.
Keep up with markets and recent deals at the banks you're targeting. Technical guides such as Mergers & Inquisitions or the BIWS 400 questions cover most of what's asked.

name: Consulting
summary: Consultants advise organizations on their hardest problems: growth, cost, operations, M&A and strategy. Most work is project-based, on teams that rotate across clients and industries.

guide.heading: What the work looks like
items: Firms advise companies across industries. Large management consultancies are generalists; boutiques specialize by industry, function or region.
Projects (cases) usually last 3–6 months, at the client's site or in the office.
Expect 50–60 hour weeks, with weekends usually protected.
Types of work: strategy, operations, M&A, technology, people and organization, risk, supply chain, sustainability, and more.
On a typical team, a partner wins the work and sets the approach, a manager runs the day-to-day and client meetings, and analysts gather and analyze data and turn it into clear recommendations.

guide.heading: Major firms
items: MBB: McKinsey, BCG and Bain, the three most prestigious strategy firms.
Big Four: Deloitte, PwC, EY (including EY-Parthenon) and KPMG, best known for audit and tax, with large consulting practices.
Others: Oliver Wyman, L.E.K., Kearney, Accenture, Alvarez & Marsal, and many specialized boutiques.

guide.heading: Why consulting
items: Exposure to many industries and to senior executives early in your career.
Real responsibility as a junior analyst, plus training in communication, Excel and structured problem solving.
A strong network and broad exits: corporate strategy, business school, private equity, startups, and the public and non-profit sectors.
Offers are very competitive, so preparation matters.

guide.heading: What firms look for
items: Strong academics (a high GPA matters more in consulting than in most fields).
Leadership and impact: roles where you can point to a result you drove.
Structured problem solving, comfort with numbers, and clear communication.
Coachability, curiosity, and being someone a team would want to work with (the "airport test").

guide.heading: Early programs
items: Many firms run freshman and sophomore programs, such as Bain's BEL, CREW and First Forward, BCG Launch, and McKinsey's first-year summits.
McKinsey uses a single "Connect with McKinsey" form as the way in to several of its programs, so fill it out early.
Several firms renamed, paused or opened up their diversity programs recently. Check the Programs tab and each firm's page for current eligibility.

guide.heading: Recruiting process
items: Deadlines for sophomore-year internship applications have moved earlier, into late winter and spring, and may keep moving earlier.
Many firms use online assessments: McKinsey Solve (game-based), BCG Casey (chatbot case) and Bain's online test. Strong scores matter for moving forward.
Interviews mix case interviews (profitability, market sizing, market entry, M&A) with behavioral questions. Final rounds are often in person.
Some firms now include AI-assisted exercises or simulated client conversations, so practice explaining your own judgment clearly.

guide.heading: Resources
items: CaseCoach (free through Vanderbilt), Management Consulted, PrepLounge, CaseInterview.com, Crafting Cases and RocketBlocks.
MBA case books for practice cases; practice live with partners as often as you can.
Vanderbilt Career Center and Handshake for on-campus recruiting; levels.fyi for pay data.

guide.heading: Entry-level pay (2026, approximate)
items: MBB: about $120k–$125k base.
Big Four consulting: about $78k–$95k base.
Other strategy firms: about $95k–$112k base (e.g., Oliver Wyman, L.E.K., Alvarez & Marsal, EY-Parthenon).

name: Software Engineering
summary: Software engineers design, build, test and maintain software, turning requirements into reliable, scalable systems. The job is changing quickly as AI tools write more code.

guide.heading: What the job is
items: Writing code, designing systems and reviewing teammates' work. It isn't coding all day: stand-ups, design reviews and meetings with product managers and designers take real time.
Teams are organized by product (search, payments, ads) or by platform (infrastructure, data, AI).
A typical day mixes a short team stand-up, a planning meeting or two, and long blocks of focused development time.

guide.heading: Who hires
items: Big Tech: Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, Apple, NVIDIA.
Fintech companies and banks' engineering teams.
Startups and AI labs, which hire at any time and vary widely in process.
Quant trading firms, as software or systems engineers.

guide.heading: How AI is changing the job
items: A large and growing share of new code at big companies is AI-generated and then reviewed by engineers.
Interviews are changing too: some companies now run AI-assisted coding rounds or code-reading rounds.

You still need strong fundamentals, but you're increasingly judged on reading code, breaking problems down and checking AI output. Interviewers notice when someone accepts buggy AI code without reviewing it.

guide.heading: When it recruits
items: SWE recruiting opens in the summer, not the spring. Most Big Tech, fintech and quant internship postings for the junior summer go up between July and September, the summer after sophomore year.
Applications are rolling, so apply in the first week a posting opens. More companies keep posting from January to April.
Freshman and sophomore programs (e.g., Explore Microsoft, NVIDIA Ignite, SEO Tech Developer) recruit earlier. See the Programs tab.
Most people apply with a resume and, ideally, a referral; cover letters are rare. A referral helps you get the first interview, and after that your performance decides.

guide.heading: Interviews
items: Online assessment: timed coding problems, auto-graded.
Technical rounds: usually 2–3 rounds of live coding where you need the right answer and a clear explanation of your approach.
Behavioral: 1–2 rounds on teamwork, conflict and learning from failure. This is where you can stand out.
In an AI-assisted round, the test is whether you check the code: read every line the AI writes, test edge cases, and say out loud what you're verifying.
Practice: "Given an array of numbers, return the two that add up to a target. What's the fastest approach?" or "Here's code an AI wrote. Find the bug and explain your fix."

guide.heading: Pay
items: Big Tech SWE interns: roughly $98k–$131k annualized, sometimes with equity.
Big Tech entry-level total compensation: about $150k–$250k, split between base salary and stock.

guide.heading: Resources
items: LeetCode for coding practice; the Simplify Summer Internships list on GitHub to track postings; r/csMajors; Levels.fyi for pay.
Set alerts on Simplify and Handshake so you see postings the week they open.

name: Product Management
summary: Product managers decide what gets built and why, then lead engineers, designers and business teams to launch it, balancing what users need, what the business needs and what engineering can build.

guide.heading: What the job is
items: Define product strategy, decide which features matter most, and guide a product from idea to launch.
PMs lead without being the boss: they persuade engineers and designers rather than manage them.
You'll like it if you care about users and strategy and enjoy running the room.

guide.heading: How people get in
items: New grads usually enter through Associate Product Manager (APM) programs: 1–2 years with rotations, mentorship and training.
APM programs are extremely selective (top programs accept a tiny fraction of applicants).
Many PMs start as engineers, analysts or consultants and switch in later, so tech-adjacent experience is valuable.

guide.heading: When it recruits
items: PM internship applications open roughly August to November of junior year. Many top APM intern roles require you to be in your second-to-last or last year.
Windows can be very short, sometimes only a week, so set alerts and apply as soon as a posting opens.
Some programs now ask for a product demo instead of a resume, and a few companies run APM tracks for students earlier in school.
New-grad APM programs typically post in early fall of senior year.

guide.heading: Interviews
items: Product sense: "Design a product for…" or "Improve X." Clarify the goal, pick a user, find their pain points and prioritize solutions.
Analytical / execution: metrics and experiments. "Signups dropped 10%, what happened?" "How would you measure success?" A/B testing.
Behavioral and technical: leadership stories (STAR method), plus enough technical understanding to discuss tradeoffs with engineers.
Usually a recruiter screen, then a first interview mixing product and analytical questions, then a final round of 3–5 interviews.
Practice: "How would you improve Vanderbilt's course registration?" or "Daily active users fell 10% overnight. Walk me through what you'd check."

guide.heading: Pay
items: PM interns: roughly $94k–$125k annualized at large tech companies (some pay hourly, around $55–$60/hour).
New-grad APMs: roughly $116k–$165k base plus equity at top programs.

guide.heading: Resources
items: APMList for program dates; Simplify's APM tracker; Exponent for interview prep; Levels.fyi for pay.
Build something people use (an app, a tool for a club) so you have real product stories to tell.

name: Sales & Trading
summary: Sales & Trading is the part of a bank that pitches trading ideas to clients and executes their trades in stocks, bonds, currencies and commodities, while managing the bank's own risk.

guide.heading: What the job is
items: S&T sits in a bank's Markets (Global Markets) division, separate from investment banking.
Sales is client-facing: building relationships with investors such as hedge funds, pension funds and asset managers, pitching ideas and taking orders. It tests communication and pitching.
Trading means making markets for clients, managing the desk's risk and positions, and pricing trades. It tests math and judgment under pressure.
Desks: Equities (stocks, equity derivatives) and FICC (fixed income such as rates and credit, currencies, commodities). Summer analyst programs often rotate you across desks before you're placed.
Hours follow the market: roughly 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., with weekends usually off. It's intense during market hours and loud and fast on the floor.

guide.heading: Who hires
items: Bulge brackets: Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JPMorganChase, Citi, Bank of America.
Foreign banks: Barclays, BNP Paribas, Société Générale, Deutsche Bank, and others.

guide.heading: S&T vs. quant trading
items: Bank S&T serves clients. Quant firms like Jane Street, Citadel Securities and Hudson River Trading trade the firm's own money using models.
Quant roles: quant trader (runs strategies, manages risk), quant researcher (finds predictive signals with statistics and ML), quant developer (builds trading and research systems).
Quant firms recruit earlier, often starting late in sophomore spring, with many more math and probability rounds (sometimes up to 8) and an in-person superday.
Pay at top quant firms is among the highest for new grads, often well above bank S&T.

guide.heading: When it recruits
items: S&T recruits alongside investment banking, about a year and a half ahead of the internship. Junior-summer applications land mostly in December through February of sophomore year.
Network in the fall of sophomore year, before applications open.
Some banks limit how many business/location combinations you can apply to each year, so choose carefully.
Some banks run sophomore S&T programs, and a few freshman insight programs are open too. See the Programs tab.

guide.heading: Interviews
items: Usually a HireVue or phone screen, then a superday.
Fit: "Why S&T?" "Sales or trading?" "Why our bank?"
Markets: Where are the S&P 500 and the 10-year Treasury yield? What moved this week, and why?
Pitch: a stock or a trade, with a long side, a short side and the risks.
Math: mental math, probability and brainteasers answered out loud, e.g. "What is 18 × 22?", "What's the angle between the clock hands at 9:30?", "If rates rise, what happens to bond prices, and why?"

guide.heading: Pay
items: S&T summer analysts: around $100k annualized at large banks.
Quant trading new grads: often several hundred thousand dollars in total compensation.

guide.heading: Resources
items: Mergers & Inquisitions and Wall Street Prep S&T guides; The Coffee Chat newsletter for recruiting updates.
Read the WSJ, Bloomberg and daily market news. Track indices, rates, oil and the dollar every day.
Practice mental math and definitions out loud with a timer.
